title: Missionization — the establishment system
subtitle: The 21 missions, their sub-stations, the Russian colony, and New Helvetia, 1769–1846
abstract: Every fixed establishment of colonial California on one map: the 21 Franciscan missions with founding years, the asistencias and estancias that extended them inland, a selected layer of the missions' named ranchos and outstations (Suisun and Napa for Sonoma, San Mateo for Dolores, Temecula and San Jacinto for San Luis Rey, and more), the Russian-American Company's fort, port, and farm ranches on the Sonoma coast, and Sutter's New Helvetia on the Sacramento. The outstation list is selected, not exhaustive: the missions ran many more ranchos. Use the timeline to watch the chain grow north and the rivals appear. Outstation and ranch locations are approximate; mission sites are exact.

features.name: Sutter's Fort (New Helvetia)
features.summary: Sutter's Mexican land-grant colony at the Sacramento-American confluence, founded 1839. Buyer of Ross's movable property in 1841, magnet for the overland emigrants, and the hinge between the mission-rancho world and the American conquest. The anti-Micheltorena revolt charged the governor with his 'relaciones secretas' with Sutter (C-A 61).

sources.citation: Standard accounts (Bancroft, Hist. Cal., IV); cf. Leg. Rec. (C-A 61) Doc 19

features.name: Royal Presidio Chapel
features.summary: Dedicated to San Carlos Borromeo — not to be confused with Mission San Carlos at Carmel. The capital's own church — the presidio chapel rebuilt in stone 1791–94, serving soldiers and vecinos under royal (not missionary) auspices; the only presidio chapel still standing. The crown furnished it: the 1794 accounts approve decorating its wall with a retablo and altar canvas.

sources.citation: Prov. State Papers (C-A 6), doc 341 — the 1794 retablo/altar approval
Bancroft, History of California I, 684–86 (the 1791–94 rebuilding)

features.notes: Drawn at the chapel site itself (today’s San Carlos Cathedral), a block from the presidio quadrangle marker.

features.name: Plaza Church (Los Ángeles)
features.summary: La Iglesia de Nuestra Señora de los Ángeles — The pueblo's own church, begun 1818 and dedicated in December 1822 — built because Los Ángeles had none: in 1810 the San Gabriel padre refused to come confess the vecinos, and the pueblo's representation went up to the Padre Presidente. The largest town in California finally got an altar of its own.

sources.citation: Prov. Records (C-A 26), doc 11 — the 1810 confession refusal and the vecinos' representation
Bancroft, History of California II, 110–11, 566–67 (construction 1818–22, dedication)

features.name: St. Joseph's Chapel
features.summary: At the Pueblo de San José: the vecinos raised its own adobe chapel in 1803, ending dependence on Mission Santa Clara three miles off — the third secular congregation of Spanish California, and the seed of today's St. Joseph's.

sources.citation: Bancroft, History of California II, 135 (the 1803 pueblo chapel) [standard record]

features.name: Presidio Chapel, Santa Bárbara
features.summary: The chapel of the Presidio de Santa Bárbara, serving the garrison and the vecinos who grew up around the quadrangle — the fourth secular congregation of Spanish California. The chapel standing today at El Presidio State Historic Park is a reconstruction on the original foundations.

sources.citation: Prov. State Papers (C-A 1), doc 183 — the 1779 founding blueprint for the Presidio del Canal de Santa Bárbara
Bancroft, History of California I (the presidio's founding, 1782) [standard record]
